inlines.value: To improve performance and reduce storage overhead, databases can use external storage for certain columns. This type of storage is used for columns that store large amounts of data, such as the PostgreSQL TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique), Oracle Large Object (LOB), or the Oracle Exadata Extended String data types. To reduce I/O overhead and increase query speed, when data changes in a table row, the database retrieves only the columns that contain new values, ignoring data in externally stored columns that remain unchanged. As a result, the value of the externally stored column is not recorded in the database log, and Debezium subsequently omits the column when it emits the event record. Downstream consumers that receive event records that omit required values can experience processing errors.
If a value for an externally stored column is not present in the database log entry for an event, when Debezium emits a record for the event, it replaces the missing value with an
sentinel value. These sentinel values are inserted into appropriately typed fields, for example, a byte array for bytes, a string for strings, or a key-value map for maps.
To retrieve data for columns that were not available in the initial query, you can apply the Debezium reselect columns post processor (

). You can configure the post processor to reselect one or more columns from a table. After you configure the post processor, it monitors events that the connector emits for the column names that you designate for reselection. When it detects an event with the specified columns, the post processor re-queries the source tables to retrieve data for the specified columns, and fetches their current state.

The reselect columns post processor generates a reselect query that returns the row to be modified. To construct the
clause for the query, by default, the post processor uses a relational table model that is based on the table’s primary key columns or on the unique index that is defined for the table.

To enable the post processor to return a consistently usable result for a keyless table, it’s best to designate a custom key that can identify a unique row. The custom key must be capable of uniquely identify records in the source table based on a combination of columns.

By default, the post processor queries the database for every event that requires reselection. For workloads in which the same rows are reselected repeatedly (for example, TOAST or LOB columns that Debezium emits as placeholders on every unrelated row update), you can enable an optional cache of reselected values to reduce the number of database queries.

. Reselected values are cached per row and per column, using the event’s message key as the cache key. Before querying the database, the post processor checks the cache for each column that requires reselection, and only queries columns that are not already cached. Eligible columns whose values are present in the event record are also written to the cache, even if no reselection is needed, so a later event that omits the same column can be served from the cache without querying the database again.

The cache is refreshed on modification: any event that carries a real (non-placeholder) value for an eligible column updates that column’s cache entry with the current value. As a result, a later event that does not modify the column can be served from the cache, and a cached value is never served after the column has changed.

Because the row identity is the message key, including its schema, a change to the key’s schema (for example, a DDL change or a primary-key reordering) yields a different cache key, so the post processor queries the database for the new key rather than returning a stale cached value.
The cache storage is pluggable through the

, stores values on the JVM heap. The cache is bounded in both dimensions, the number of rows and the number of columns cached per row, and evicts the least-recently-used entries when a bound is exceeded. Cached values also expire after a time-to-live, which bounds how long entries for rows that are no longer being updated are retained in memory. The cache is lost when the connector stops, so reselections begin repopulating it after a restart.
The in-memory cache supports the following properties, in addition to the common
The maximum number of cached rows retained in the reselection cache.
When the limit is reached, the least-recently-used entries are evicted.
The time-to-live, in milliseconds, of a cached reselection value.

Because the cache is refreshed on modification, this value only bounds how long entries for rows that are no longer being updated are retained in memory; it is not the mechanism that guarantees freshness.
The maximum number of columns cached per row in the reselection cache.

When the limit is reached, the least-recently-used column entries for that row are evicted. This bound guards against wide tables (for example, tables with 500-1000 columns) growing the per-row inner map without limit.

implementation persists cached values to disk in an embedded RocksDB database. Cached values persist after you a connector restarts, so columns that would otherwise need to be reselected continue to be served from the cache after a restart. Entries remain correct across restarts because the post processor refreshes the cache whenever a column arrives with a real value.
To use the RocksDB cache, the

Storage is permanent by default: no time-to-live is applied, and the database directory is retained when the connector stops. If you specify a positive

value, expired entries are treated as cache misses and removed when they are read. RocksDB reclaims expired entries from disk during compaction. A time-to-live is recommended for schemas that change frequently, because entries written under a previous key schema are never overwritten and would otherwise remain on disk indefinitely.
The time-to-live setting determines how the RocksDB database is opened, and the two modes store entries on disk in different formats. If you change

and a positive value across a connector restart, entries that were written before the change can become unreadable in the new mode. Unreadable entries are discarded and treated as cache misses, so the affected columns are transparently reselected from the database and re-cached; no manual cleanup of the storage directory is required.

Specifies whether the RocksDB database directory is deleted when the connector stops.
By default the directory is retained, so cached values persist across connector restarts.

Note that this is the same property that the in-memory cache uses, but with a different default: persistent storage is permanent unless a time-to-live is explicitly configured.
